title: The foreach Statement
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of the foreach statement in a C#/.NET program.
Predict the result of the included C# example and verify the documented output.
Apply the foreach statement to a small task and identify one relevant boundary, limitation, or version requirement.

content.intro: The foreach Statement is lesson 42 in Input, Output, and Control Flow. Control flow decides which statements execute and how repetition progresses. Verify branch boundaries and termination conditions.
content.why_it_matters: Programs become useful when they can make decisions and respond to input, including invalid input. This lesson focuses on the foreach statement and shows how to verify the behavior instead of relying on assumptions.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Control flow decides which statements execute and how repetition progresses. Verify branch boundaries and termination conditions.

content_blocks.title: A practical way to learn it
content_blocks.text: Start with the smallest valid case for the foreach statement. Predict the output, run or inspect the example in the stated toolchain, then change one input or rule and compare the result. For production code, record assumptions and verify boundary cases.

items.title: Iterating over arrays
items.text: Check bounds and copy behavior. Index-from-end and ranges make positions concise but do not remove boundary requirements.

items.title: Iterating over collections
items.text: For iterating over collections, define the expected behavior, inspect how it relates to the foreach statement, and verify a representative case plus one boundary or failure case.

items.title: Iteration variables
items.text: A variable has a type, a current value, and a scope. Initialize it before use, limit its lifetime where possible, and make state changes visible so later code can reason about it.

items.title: foreach vs indexed loops
items.text: Check initialization, termination, and progress together; every loop needs a clear path to completion or cancellation.

items.title: Enumeration and iteration concepts
items.text: Check initialization, termination, and progress together; every loop needs a clear path to completion or cancellation.

content.task: Try it yourself: create a small C# example that demonstrates the foreach statement. Change one input or implementation detail, predict the result, then check it locally and explain one edge case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates the foreach statement rather than only repeating its definition.
The result is checked locally or against a clearly documented reference output.
At least one relevant boundary, invalid-input case, or compatibility condition is considered.
hints: List the assumptions and expected behavior for the foreach statement before editing the code.
Change one variable or rule at a time; keep the previous output for comparison.
If behavior differs, confirm the compiler/target framework and consult the linked official documentation.
content.solution_notes: Suggested approach: identify the expected input and output, start from the smallest example, use the feature only where it clarifies the rule, and verify both a typical case and a boundary/failure case.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming the feature works identically on every target
common_mistakes.why: Language syntax, libraries, and runtime support are version-dependent.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the target framework and official versioned reference before using the feature.

common_mistakes.why: Boundary values, malformed input, and failure states often expose the real bug.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one typical input and one boundary or invalid case to the manual or automated checks.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating sample output as proof that the code ran
common_mistakes.why: The course reader uses static reference output for C# because it has no C# execution runner.
common_mistakes.fix: Run the snippet in a local .NET project or a separately isolated execution service.
